newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks post modest gains.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks post modest gains.

text.p: Upbeat January retail sales reports drove blue-chip stocks higher Thursday, but investors were cautious ahead of Friday's report on January employment figures.
The dollar hit 124 Japanese yen for the first time in four years and also gained against Germany's mark. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond dropped.
In commodity markets, oil prices fell amid warmer weather in the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market.

The 30-stock Dow Jones industrial average closed up 26.16 points at 6,773.06. In the broader market, advances led declines 1,233 to 1,219 on active volume of 519 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"Several retailing companies gave us better-than-expected numbers, and we got some good activity in the group for the first time in a long time," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
Analysts said apparel stores reported standout results, with chain stores such as Gap Inc. and Limited Inc. as well as key department stores posting strong numbers.

The buying interest was clearly tempered, however, as investors warily awaited key employment and wage data due Friday morning before the stock market opens. Markets often respond violently to surprises in the report, considered a key leading indicator of inflation.
Analysts said any gain of more than 275,000 jobs in non-farm payrolls could trigger a sell-off in financial markets.
The concern is that with the jobless rate declining, there could be a buildup in inflationary pressures stemming from a tight labour market and stepped-up wage demands by workers.

Economists surveyed by Reuters expect the report to show the unemployment rate declined slightly in January to 5.2 percent from 5.3 percent in December, while average hourly wages are expected to show a modest 0.2 percent increase.

Almost forgotten by the end of the session was the highly awaited release early in the day of President Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget. The budget blueprint was considered a test of credibility on the path to a balanced federal budget by 2002.
Stocks showed little response to the presentation, even though many Wall Street professionals criticised the budget's assumptions.
In the bond market, the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond dipped 1/32, or 31 cents on a $1,000 bond. The yield held steady at 6.76 percent.

In currency markets, the dollar surged briefly to 124 yen and to 1.6548 marks in Europe and then retreated. In late New York trading, the dollar was at 123.75 yen, up from 123.30 yen Wednesday. The dollar fetched 1.6525 marks, up from 1.6430 German marks.

The dollar rose on hopes that finance officials from leading industrial nations will aim for stable currency rates when they convene in Berlin Saturday for a weekend meeting, as well as a belief that German interest rates may soon drop.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices dropped sharply based on views that heating oil supplies are more than ample amid declining demand and unseasonably mild weather.
March heating oil ended 1.87 cents lower at 61.45 cents a gallon, with March gasoline closing down 2.24 cents at 65.30 cents a gallon, and March crude oil down 81 cents at $23.10 a barrel.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index of leading shares closed 15.6 points down at 4,265.9. Tokyo's Nikkei 225 average ended 147.54 points lower at 18,038.43.
